title: Balance
objective: After this level you can explain how the inner ear keeps you balanced.
summary: Three fluid-filled canals in the inner ear sense head turns; tiny grains in two pouches feel gravity. When ears and eyes disagree, you get dizziness or motion sickness.

cards.headline: Spin in circles, stop, and the room keeps turning.
cards.body: You've stopped. Your eyes can see you've stopped. Something inside your head disagrees. That something is Level 61's missing sense, balance, and it lives right next door to your hearing.

cards.headline: Three loops of fluid
cards.body: Your balance organ, the vestibular system, is a maze of bone and soft tissue in your inner ear. It holds three fluid-filled semicircular canals, looped at roughly right angles to each other. When you turn your head, the fluid moves and bends hair cells, the same kind of sensor you hear with, which tells your brain which way you turned. Nod, shake or tilt, and the fluid reports it.

cards.headline: Tiny stones that feel gravity
cards.body: Two small pouches, the utricle and the saccule, sense which way is down. Their hair cells sit under a gel holding tiny grains of calcium carbonate. Gravity pulls on the grains and bends the hair cells, telling your brain if you're upright, leaning back or lying down. You carry a built-in spirit level, and it runs on tiny stones.

cards.headline: When the reports disagree
cards.body: Your brain builds balance from your eyes, your inner ears and the muscles and touch sensors in your legs. After spinning, canal fluid keeps moving though you've stopped: ears say motion, eyes say still, and you feel dizzy. Below deck on a ship it flips. Your inner ear feels the motion, your eyes see a still cabin, and that clash is the leading explanation for motion sickness.

cards.headline: Balance: steadied
learned: Three fluid-filled canals sense head turns
The utricle and saccule use tiny grains to feel gravity
Balance blends eyes, inner ears and leg sensors
Clashing signals cause dizziness and motion sickness

questions.prompt: Which parts of the inner ear tell your brain that your head is turning?

options.label: The utricle and the saccule
options.rationale: They sense gravity and which way is down.

options.label: The eardrum and the stapes
options.rationale: Those pass sound on for hearing.

questions.explanation: When your head turns, fluid in the three semicircular canals moves and bends hair cells, signaling the turn.

questions.prompt: Why do you feel dizzy right after you stop spinning?

options.label: Your eyes stop sending signals for a while
options.rationale: Your eyes correctly show you're still.

options.label: Canal fluid keeps moving, so ears and eyes disagree
The grains in your inner ear dissolve
options.rationale: The grains stay put; gravity keeps pulling on them.

options.label: Blood drains out of your inner ear for a moment
options.rationale: The cause is moving canal fluid.

questions.explanation: The fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving after you stop, so your inner ear reports motion while your eyes report stillness.

questions.prompt: From Level 60: when your brain weighs reports from your eyes, inner ears and legs to judge balance, which of its three jobs is that?

options.label: Sensation
options.rationale: Sensation is the receptors picking up the reports; weighing them comes next.

options.label: Response
options.rationale: Response is the motor message sent out afterwards.

questions.explanation: Weighing several reports against each other is integration, the step between sensation and response.
